HTTP Requests & Responses

Understand HTTP methods, URLs, headers, cookies, status codes, request bodies, and why HTTP is the foundation of practical web security testing.

Beginner22 min
Why this matters

HTTP is the language through which browsers and web applications exchange requests and responses. For security testing, read the HTTP message rather than treating a web page as a black box. A request can contain a method, path, query parameters, headers, cookies, and a body. A response can contain a status code, headers, cookies, and content. Small differences often reveal authentication, authorization, caching, validation, or routing behavior.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • The client sends a request such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE to a URL.
  • The request can contain query parameters, headers, cookies, and a body. Treat values supplied by the client as untrusted unless the server independently verifies them.
  • A server or intermediary processes the request and returns a response with a status code, headers, cookies, and content.
  • Cookies can make stateless HTTP participate in stateful sessions, so security depends on how session identifiers are generated, transmitted, scoped, and invalidated.
  • Reverse proxies, CDNs, and caches can introduce additional parsing and trust boundaries, so the same request should not automatically be assumed to mean the same thing at every layer.

The background

HTTP originated as a simple protocol for transferring hypermedia and has evolved through HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. Its headers, methods, caching behavior, cookies, authentication mechanisms, and proxy ecosystem are fundamental to modern applications.

Real-world examples

  • MDN describes HTTP as a client-server protocol where clients send requests and servers return responses; understanding that flow is foundational for web debugging and security testing.
  • Security issues such as request smuggling, cache poisoning, authentication weaknesses, and Host-header problems can arise when different components interpret HTTP messages differently.

What to look for

  • Identify the method, path, query string, Host header, cookies, authorization headers, content type, and body.
  • Record how status codes and response bodies change when one input changes.
  • Check which values are reflected, stored, used for routing, used for authorization, or passed to another component.
  • Compare browser-visible behavior with the underlying request and response.
  • Pay attention to Set-Cookie attributes such as Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use HTTPS consistently and configure secure transport correctly.
  • Parse and validate HTTP messages consistently across front-end and back-end components.
  • Set appropriate cookie attributes and avoid placing sensitive data in URLs when a safer mechanism is available.
  • Return appropriate status codes without exposing unnecessary implementation details.
  • Define explicit cache behavior for sensitive responses and test proxy/CDN behavior.
  • Use a well-tested framework HTTP stack rather than implementing protocol parsing yourself.
